questions.prompt: What primary data structure does VoiceOver use to read your user interface?

options.text: The accessibility tree provided by UIKit and SwiftUI.
options.explanation: VoiceOver walks the semantic accessibility tree rather than raw screen pixels.

options.text: The raw pixel buffer rendered by Core Animation layers.
options.explanation: Screen readers do not inspect GPU pixel framebuffers directly.

options.text: The optical character recognition scanner inside iOS.
options.explanation: iOS uses accessibility metadata rather than running OCR on normal views.

options.text: The internal Auto Layout constraint equation graph.
options.explanation: Constraints position views visually, but VoiceOver reads the accessibility tree.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the accessibilityLabel property on an element?

options.text: It defines the font size used by Dynamic Type text engines.
options.explanation: Dynamic Type font scaling uses font metrics, not accessibility labels.

options.text: It provides a short and descriptive name for the control.
options.explanation: The accessibility label gives VoiceOver users a clear name for the element.

options.text: It lists all internal subviews contained inside the view hierarchy.
options.explanation: The label does not enumerate subview hierarchies.

options.text: It triggers haptic feedback whenever the user touches the view.
options.explanation: Haptics use UIFeedbackGenerator, not accessibility labels.

questions.prompt: What does the accessibilityValue property represent to assistive technologies?

options.text: The monetary price of an in-app purchase item.
options.explanation: accessibilityValue describes element state, not financial pricing.

options.text: The hex color code used to fill the background layer.
options.explanation: accessibilityValue communicates current control state rather than colors.

options.text: The current state or numerical quantity of the control.
options.explanation: Values indicate current progress, slider amounts, or active choices.

options.text: The unique database identifier assigned to the user profile.
options.explanation: Database identifiers belong in data models, not in accessibility values.

questions.prompt: Which accessibility property communicates element behavior such as being a button or a header?

options.text: The accessibilityIdentifier string used for UI testing.
options.explanation: accessibilityIdentifier is for automated tests and is never spoken.

options.text: The accessibilityHint string explaining interaction steps.
options.explanation: Hints explain action results, while traits describe control types.

options.text: The accessibilityLanguage property specifying locale codes.
options.explanation: accessibilityLanguage sets pronunciation language, not control traits.

options.text: The accessibilityTraits bitmask defining element capabilities.
options.explanation: Traits tell VoiceOver whether an element is a button, header, link, or image.

questions.prompt: When is it appropriate to provide an accessibilityHint for a user interface control?

options.text: When the result of tapping the control is not obvious from the label.
options.explanation: Hints clarify the outcome when a simple name is not enough.

options.text: On every single button and label across the entire app.
options.explanation: Excessive hints clutter navigation and slow down VoiceOver users.

options.text: Only when the view is completely hidden from visual rendering.
options.explanation: Hidden views should not have accessibility hints.

options.text: When you want VoiceOver to skip speaking the accessibility label.
options.explanation: Hints do not replace accessibility labels; they follow after them.

questions.prompt: In what order does VoiceOver announce element metadata when focusing on a control?

options.text: Hint first, then trait, and finally label.
options.explanation: VoiceOver announces the name first, not the hint.

options.text: Label first, then trait, followed by hint after a pause.
options.explanation: VoiceOver presents name, type, and optional guidance in natural sequence.

options.text: Trait first, then value, and finally label.
options.explanation: Traits are spoken after the element label.

options.text: Only the accessibility identifier is announced.
options.explanation: Identifiers are never spoken aloud by VoiceOver.

options.explanation: VoiceOver does not blur the window during normal navigation.

options.explanation: VoiceOver highlights the focused item with a distinct accessibility cursor.

questions.prompt: What does accessibilityElement(children: .combine) do in SwiftUI?

options.text: It groups child views into a single accessible element for VoiceOver.
options.explanation: Combining children allows users to read compound views with a single swipe.

options.text: It merges all subviews into a single Core Graphics image bitmap.
options.explanation: Combining children affects accessibility nodes, not graphic rasterization.

options.text: It removes all labels and hides the view from screen readers.
options.explanation: To hide elements, use accessibilityHidden(true) or .ignore.

options.text: It converts text strings into localized catalog keys automatically.
options.explanation: Localization is handled by String catalogs, not accessibility grouping.

questions.prompt: When should you use accessibilityElement(children: .ignore) in SwiftUI?

options.text: When you want VoiceOver to read every child subview individually.
options.explanation: Reading children individually is the default behavior without ignore.

options.text: When you want to replace child accessibility nodes with a custom container label.
options.explanation: Using .ignore drops child nodes so you can attach custom accessibility attributes.

options.text: When an app enters background mode to save memory.
options.explanation: Accessibility modifiers apply to active view hierarchies.

options.text: When preparing SwiftUI views for export as PDF documents.
options.explanation: Accessibility modifiers configure assistive technology, not document printing.

questions.prompt: How should custom multi-finger gestures or swipe actions be exposed to VoiceOver users?

options.text: By requiring users to disable VoiceOver before swiping.
options.explanation: Assistive users must never be told to disable screen readers.

options.text: By embedding long instruction paragraphs inside the accessibility label.
options.explanation: Labels must remain concise; instructions do not substitute for actions.

options.text: By adding custom accessibility actions accessible through the Rotor.
options.explanation: Custom actions let VoiceOver users trigger actions via the Rotor menu.

options.text: By replacing all gestures with hardware volume button clicks.
options.explanation: Hardware buttons cannot replace accessible software gestures.

questions.prompt: What mistake occurs if you set a button accessibilityLabel to 'Bookmark button'?

options.text: The app crashes due to an invalid character in the string.
options.explanation: The word button is valid text and will not crash the app.

options.text: VoiceOver refuses to speak any label longer than one word.
options.explanation: VoiceOver reads multiple words without issues.

options.text: The button stops accepting user touch interactions.
options.explanation: Accessibility labels do not alter touch hit testing.

options.text: VoiceOver speaks redundant text like 'Bookmark button, button'.
options.explanation: Because traits already announce 'button', repeating it produces duplicate speech.

questions.prompt: How should purely decorative background images be handled for VoiceOver in SwiftUI?

options.text: Mark them with accessibilityHidden(true) or use Image(decorative:).
options.explanation: Hiding decorative images keeps the accessibility tree clean and uncluttered.

options.text: Provide an empty string for the accessibilityHint property.
options.explanation: An empty hint does not hide the element from VoiceOver.

options.text: Set their opacity to 0.01 to trick the system renderer.
options.explanation: Opacity hacks still leave elements present in the accessibility tree.

options.text: Assign the button trait to make them tap targets.
options.explanation: Decorative items should never be marked as interactive buttons.

questions.prompt: What should you do in UIKit when presenting a custom non-modal dialog to update VoiceOver focus?

options.text: Restart the UIApplication run loop to clear memory.
options.explanation: The run loop cannot be restarted manually.

options.text: Post UIAccessibility.post with screenChanged and the new view.
options.explanation: Posting screenChanged tells VoiceOver to shift focus to the new dialog element.

options.text: Delete all subviews from the key UIWindow.
options.explanation: Deleting subviews destroys the interface.

options.text: Trigger a silent push notification via APNs.
options.explanation: Push notifications are for remote delivery, not local focus updates.

questions.prompt: Explain the differences between accessibilityLabel, accessibilityValue, and accessibilityHint in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that accessibilityLabel provides the name or description of the control
Explains that accessibilityValue conveys current state or amount
Explains that accessibilityHint gives additional guidance on interaction results

questions.modelAnswer: The accessibilityLabel provides a concise name identifying the element, such as 'Volume'. In contrast, accessibilityValue describes the current numerical or state value of that element, such as '75 percent'. Finally, accessibilityHint offers optional guidance explaining what occurs upon interaction when the outcome is not obvious.

questions.prompt: Explain why and when you should use accessibilityElement(children: .combine) in SwiftUI in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that .combine merges child accessibility elements into a single spoken unit
Explains that this improves navigation efficiency on compound views like cards or list rows

questions.modelAnswer: You use accessibilityElement(children: .combine) on container views like cards or custom list cells containing multiple text views. Instead of forcing VoiceOver users to swipe through each label separately, .combine merges all child labels into a single accessible unit. This drastically reduces repetitive swipes and makes navigation much faster.

questions.prompt: Explain why you should never include control type words like 'button' or 'image' inside an accessibility label in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that accessibility traits already announce control type automatically
Explains that repeating the type results in redundant, confusing speech like 'Play button, button'

questions.modelAnswer: You should never include control words like 'button' or 'image' in an accessibility label because accessibility traits announce the control type automatically. If a developer labels a button as 'Play button', VoiceOver speaks both the label and trait, resulting in 'Play button, button'. Keeping the label as 'Play' allows VoiceOver to convey a clean, professional sentence.

questions.prompt: Explain how to manage screen reader focus when presenting a custom dialog or dynamic view in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Mentions posting UIAccessibility notifications like screenChanged or layoutChanged in UIKit
Explains passing the target element to shift VoiceOver focus or using AccessibilityFocusState in SwiftUI

questions.modelAnswer: When presenting a custom dialog, you must explicitly notify assistive technologies about the screen transition. In UIKit, call UIAccessibility.post with notification .screenChanged and pass the dialog view as the argument to guide focus. In SwiftUI, bind the dialog to an AccessibilityFocusState property to move VoiceOver cursor directly to the new content.

questions.prompt: Explain how a senior iOS developer designs accessibility into an app from the start in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Discusses integrating accessibility into foundational design systems like minimum 44pt touch targets and Dynamic Type
Discusses custom Rotor actions and automated accessibility audits in CI with Xcode or XCTest

questions.modelAnswer: A senior developer treats accessibility as a foundational architectural requirement within the design system. This includes enforcing 44-point minimum touch targets, supporting Dynamic Type without clipping, and creating custom Rotor actions for gesture shortcuts. Finally, they add automated accessibility audits to continuous integration using XCTest to prevent regressions before shipping.
